headline: Jonathan Takadina holds Yancoal but prefers New Hope and Aurizon for coal exposure
reasoning: Jonathan is critical of Yancoal's decision around 18 months to two years ago not to pay a dividend, which he sees as an own goal given the ESG-constrained investor base for coal stocks. With the stock near lows, he would not initiate a position here and instead prefers New Hope (consistent dividend payer) and Aurizon (owns Queensland coal rail infrastructure, steady run and good dividend) as better ways to access steady ~$100/tonne thermal coal.
quote: Yann Collis pretty much kicked an own goal, I think about 18 months ago or two years when they declared no dividend. Like, it was the point of having a coal stock when it doesn't pay out dividends... if I was to invest in the coal space, I'd rather be in other areas in there. So New Hope, decent operators pay a consistent dividend. But the other one at the moment is AZJ. So they actually were old Queensland Rail. But basically, they own all of the coal rail infrastructure within Queensland.
episode_title: technicals & fundamentals | the call: Monday 10 August

headline: Paradice retains Yancoal overweight as part of energy security theme despite -33.7% fall, citing fortress balance sheet and attractive valuation.
reasoning: YAL fell -33.7% in a mirror image of the March quarter, when it was one of the top contributors. As ceasefire negotiations progressed, emergency gas-to-coal switching demand that drove the spike in seaborne thermal coal unwound rapidly, with Newcastle benchmark prices giving back the entire March rally. The fund took profits near the highs, reducing the position early in the quarter, which mitigated but did not eliminate the impact. YAL remains attractively valued, with a fortress balance sheet and strong cash generation, and the fund retains a holding as part of its energy security theme.
quote: YAL fell -33.7% in a mirror image of the March quarter, when it was one of our top contributors. As ceasefire negotiations progressed, the emergency gas-to-coal switching demand that drove the spike in seaborne thermal coal unwound rapidly – Newcastle benchmark prices gave back the entire March rally (Thermal Coal finished the quarter down -9.0%, with LNG down -20.3%, both in USD). We took profits near the highs, reducing the position early in the quarter, which mitigated but did not eliminate the impact. YAL remains attractively valued, with a fortress balance sheet and strong cash generation, and we retain a holding as part of our energy security theme.
episode_title: Small Cap Ops Fund Factsheet June 2026

headline: David Bird holds Yancoal with a bullish long-term energy thesis but would only re-enter around $4.40-$4.45
reasoning: Bird is bullish on the energy sector over the coming decade, particularly given AI data center demand and global energy deficits, and sees coal as part of that bull market. The Kestrel acquisition strengthened Yancoal's balance sheet and supports reliable dividends. However, he recently sold after buyers failed to sustain the breakout, and would only re-enter around the $4.40-$4.45 support zone if buyers step up there.
quote: It was looking really, really good at the beginning of the year when it broke out to that new high. And I have to admit, I was actually on it then, but I actually sold it recently, once it started to come back in. Because once those sellers didn't become buyers, I became very cautious. And right now, it's in this mid range. I'd be kind of looking to see if it gets down to that kind of $4.45 range. And if those buyers start to step up there, that's where I might become interested again. So I'd say to hold for now, but it is one that I believe will go high in the long run. I'm very bullish on the energy sector in the coming decade.
episode_title: technicals vs fundamentals | the call: Thursday 25 June

headline: Howard Coleman avoids Yancoal due to inability to predict coal prices and regulatory headwinds on expansion
reasoning: Coleman acknowledges Yancoal offers a decent dividend on a PE of 15 and generates strong cash flow, but places it in the 'too hard' basket because coal prices are inherently unpredictable. He also notes Australian government policy makes expansion difficult, limiting long-term growth. Team Invest requires around 85% earnings visibility over five years, which coal companies cannot provide. The structural global coal demand story is real, but the investment case fails his filters.
quote: The problem with coal companies in Australia particularly is firstly, we don't know what's going to happen to the coal price. Anybody who tells you in advance what a commodity price is going to be doing sometime well into the future is either guessing or dishonest because there's no way of knowing. So where's the long-term growth coming from? But you do get quite a decent dividend because it's on a reasonably low PE ratio of 15. So if you're looking for a dividend and you think the coal price will stay high, Yancoal may be a good one, but they go in the too hard basket for team investment members because we can't predict.
episode_title: technicals vs fundamentals | the call: Thursday 25 June
